findings.title: Returned binary identity can describe bytes other than the packaged member
findings.root_cause: The archive member is captured from binary.read_bytes() at line 40, but binary_sha256 reopens the live source path at line 79 after the archive has been written and verified. There is no equality or stability check between those reads.
findings.reproduction: review_probe.py replaces the isolated source binary immediately after package_native hashes the completed archive and before it hashes the source path for binary_sha256. The generated archive retains the old bytes (SHA-256 66bb09e4699bf6d7b7033b395b33bdc2d4152f592ee2150fb996275683f7b6be), while the returned binary_sha256 is for the new bytes (b01e58dd4236667fb0254a1b9e67bde1c972b9a6fabd3d6e3333d7d6b71824a5).
findings.impact: The archive checksum remains valid, but package identity metadata can bind it to the wrong executable identity. A build or release audit that trusts the returned binary_sha256 can therefore claim provenance for bytes that are not in the archive.
findings.minimal_direction: Hash the already captured contents["llmgw"] bytes for binary_sha256. That directly binds the reported identity to the member that was verified in the tar and needs no new locking or abstraction.

findings.title: Failed-replacement recovery can delete a concurrently written target
findings.root_cause: Recovery only recognizes the original previous hash as safe. When a backup exists and the current target is anything else, lines 112-115 remove that target unconditionally before moving the backup. The script has no installer lock or compare-and-swap at this point.
findings.reproduction: Source interleaving: start with target A and previousHash(A); File.Replace installs candidate B and creates backup A; another writer replaces target B with C before line 97; line 97 observes C != stagedHash and throws; line 108 rejects C as previous A; lines 112-115 delete C and move backup A into its place. The installer then reports the previous executable preserved even though it destroyed the concurrent writer's target.
findings.impact: A recovery path can overwrite an executable it no longer owns, contradicting the documented no-concurrent-writer and never-blindly-overwrite recovery boundary. This host had no PowerShell, so native Windows execution is not claimed.
findings.minimal_direction: If a recovery target exists with an identity other than the staged or known previous binary, preserve target, backup, and candidate and return recovery_unconfirmed. Never remove an unknown current target automatically; restore only after the expected identity and writer state are established.
